title: How to start a movement
speaker: Derek Sivers

keyTerms.definition: a group of people working together for an idea or a change
a person who supports and copies a leader
to laugh at someone in an unkind way
when something keeps growing and moving forward

predictionQuestion: How does a movement start? Who do you think matters most: the leader or the followers?

keyIdeas.text: The talk watches a movement happen from start to finish, then takes lessons from it.
A leader needs the courage to stand out and be laughed at.
What the leader is doing should be easy to follow.
The first follower has a crucial role: they show everyone else how to follow.
The leader should treat the first follower as an equal, so it's about the group, not the leader.
The first follower is what turns a "lone nut" into a leader.
A movement must be public. New followers copy the other followers, not the leader.
As more people join, there is momentum. This is the tipping point.
As the crowd grows, joining becomes less risky, so people who were waiting join too.
Biggest lesson: leadership is over-glorified. Have the courage to follow, and be the first to join someone doing something great.

modelNotes: HOW TO START A MOVEMENT (D. Sivers, TED)
- needs guts → stand out, be ridiculed
- movement must be public; new followers copy followers
- bigger crowd → less risky → others join
- leadership over-glorified → have courage to FOLLOW + be 1st to join
